title: Kachru's Model and World Englishes
subtitle: Narrativ versjon
description: A story about a deceptively simple question -- who really owns English? -- and the famous three-circle model one linguist drew to map the answer across the whole planet.
competenceGoals: analyze the position of English in the world and discuss the difference between English as a native language, English as a second language and English as a foreign language
reflect on the role of English in international contexts

content.content:
## Who Owns English?

Here is a question that sounds simple but turns out to be surprisingly deep: who *owns* the English language? With 1.5 billion speakers spread across every continent, where is the "correct" English spoken? In London? In New York? In New Delhi? In Lagos? Each of those cities would give you a different answer, and each would be convinced it was right.

The field known as **World Englishes** challenges the whole idea that there is one single "proper" English. Instead, it recognises that English has branched out into many legitimate varieties, each with its own grammar, pronunciation, vocabulary, and cultural flavour. The most influential map of this diversity was drawn in 1985 by the Indian-American linguist **Braj Kachru**, who pictured the world's English speakers as three concentric circles. Understanding his model -- and its limits -- will change how you think about your own English.

## Kachru's Three Circles

Kachru imagined English speakers arranged in three rings around a centre.

The **Inner Circle** -- around 400 million speakers -- includes countries where English is the primary native language: the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and Ireland. These countries are traditionally seen as **"norm-providing"**: they set the standards for what counts as "correct" English and are home to the major dictionaries, grammar guides, and testing organisations.

The **Outer Circle** -- around 750 million speakers -- includes countries where English was introduced through colonialism and now has an official or institutional role: India, Nigeria, Singapore, the Philippines, Kenya, South Africa, Pakistan, and Malaysia. These are described as **"norm-developing"**: they are creating their own recognised varieties of English, which live alongside local languages.

The **Expanding Circle** -- 750 million or more learners -- includes countries where English is learned as a foreign language with no colonial history: Norway, Germany, China, Japan, Brazil, Russia, and South Korea. These are traditionally **"norm-dependent"**, looking to Inner Circle standards, and they form the fastest-growing group of English users in the world. Norway sits firmly here: even though Norwegians rank among the best non-native English speakers on Earth, their relationship to English is fundamentally different from that of India or Nigeria, where colonial history gave English an official role.

In practice, the circles produce strikingly different Englishes. Inner Circle English already splits into American versus British forms (*apartment/flat*, *truck/lorry*, *color/colour*). Outer Circle Indian English has invented words like *prepone* (the opposite of postpone) and grammatical patterns like "I am having a doubt." Nigerian Pidgin English is spoken by over 75 million people, and Singapore's lively *Singlish* produces expressions like "Can lah!"

options.text: placeholder

questions.task: Which circle does Norway belong to in Kachru's model?

options.text: The Inner Circle, because Norwegians speak English so well
The Outer Circle, because English is taught in all schools
Norway fits no circle at all
The Expanding Circle -- English is a foreign language with no colonial connection

questions.solution: Norway is in the Expanding Circle because English is learned as a foreign language without a colonial connection. High proficiency does not change the circle -- the relationship to English is what matters.

questions.task: What does it mean that the Inner Circle is 'norm-providing'?

options.text: These countries traditionally set the standards for 'correct' English
They forbid all other varieties of English
They learn English only as a foreign language
They have the fewest English speakers

questions.solution: Inner Circle countries (UK, USA, etc.) are seen as norm-providing because they have traditionally set the standards and produced the major dictionaries and testing organisations.

questions.task: Which is an example of an Outer Circle English innovation?

options.text: The British spelling 'colour'
The Indian English word 'prepone', meaning the opposite of postpone
The American word 'apartment'
The Old English word 'thorn'

questions.solution: Outer Circle varieties such as Indian English create their own legitimate innovations -- 'prepone' follows logical English word-formation rules but does not exist in British or American English.

content.content:
## The Cracks in the Model

Kachru's three circles are useful, but they have been heavily criticised -- and learning the criticisms is just as important as learning the model.

First, the **boundaries are too rigid**. Reality is messier than three neat rings. Where does South Africa belong, with both native speakers and second-language speakers? And countries like the Netherlands and Scandinavia have such high English proficiency that some scholars argue they are drifting from the Expanding toward the Outer Circle. Second, the model **ignores internal diversity**. The USA (Inner Circle) contains millions of people for whom English is a second language, while India (Outer Circle) has regions where English is barely spoken and others where it dominates. Third, and most importantly, the model **implies a hierarchy**. By saying the Inner Circle "provides" norms, the Outer Circle "develops" them, and the Expanding Circle "depends" on them, it can suggest that British and American English are the real, correct standard against which everything else is measured. This marginalises the perfectly legitimate varieties of the Outer and Expanding Circles and casts their speakers as eternal "learners" rather than confident "users." Fourth, the model is **static in a dynamic world**: global migration and digital communication blur the categories. A Nigerian living in London or a Japanese person working in Singapore does not fit neatly into any one circle.

This is why some scholars now prefer concepts like **English as a Lingua Franca** or **translanguaging**, which focus on how English is actually used in the moment rather than where its speakers happen to come from. The deeper point of World Englishes is liberating: there is no single "correct" English. Each variety reflects its speakers' culture, history, and needs. The real question is not "Which English is best?" but "Which English is appropriate for this context?"

options.text: placeholder

questions.task: What is the most serious criticism of Kachru's model?

options.text: It was invented too recently to trust
It has far too many circles
It implies a hierarchy with Inner Circle English as the 'correct' standard
It ignores native speakers completely

questions.solution: A major criticism is that the model implies a hierarchy -- Inner Circle 'provides', Outer 'develops', Expanding 'depends' -- which marginalises legitimate non-native varieties and casts their speakers as perpetual learners.

questions.task: Why is South Africa a difficult case for the three-circle model?

options.text: No one there speaks English
It was never colonised
English is illegal there
It has both native English speakers and second-language speakers

questions.solution: South Africa blurs the boundaries because it has a substantial native English-speaking population alongside many second-language speakers, showing that the rigid circles do not capture reality well.

questions.task: What does the World Englishes perspective conclude about correctness?

options.text: There is no single correct English -- the question is which is appropriate for the context
Only British English is truly correct
Only Inner Circle English should be taught
All non-native English is simply wrong

questions.solution: World Englishes holds that no variety is inherently superior. The useful question is which English fits a given context and audience -- not which is universally 'best'.

questions.task: Which newer concepts do some scholars prefer over the rigid circles?

options.text: The Great Vowel Shift and inflection
English as a Lingua Franca and translanguaging
Colonialism and soft power
Old English and Middle English

questions.solution: Concepts like English as a Lingua Franca and translanguaging focus on how English is actually used in interaction, rather than on fixed geographic categories.

content.content:
## Summary

The question "Who owns English?" has no single answer, and that is the whole point of **World Englishes**. **Braj Kachru's Three Circles model** (1985) offers a helpful starting map: the **Inner Circle** of native-speaking, norm-providing nations; the **Outer Circle** of former colonies where English has an official, norm-developing role; and the **Expanding Circle** of countries like Norway that learn English as a foreign language. But the model has real limits -- its boundaries are too rigid, it ignores diversity within countries, it implies a hierarchy that unfairly favours Inner Circle English, and it struggles with our mobile, digital world. That is why scholars increasingly turn to ideas like English as a Lingua Franca and translanguaging. The liberating conclusion is that no English is inherently "correct"; each variety is valid, and the real question is always which English suits the context and audience at hand.
